## Methods

Laser stabilization
The 895 nm probe laser frequency was stabilized using saturated absorption spectroscopy to the 6S_{1/2}, F=4 \rightarrow 6P_{1/2}, F=3 transition. A portion of the 895 nm probe and the 636 nm dressing lasers were utilized to generate a two-photon EIT. The 636 nm dressing laser was tuned and locked to the 6P_{1/2}, F=3 \rightarrow 9S_{1/2}, F=4 transition using the two-photon EIT. The 2235 nm coupling laser was free running and scanned over 4 GHz to access the various Rydberg states prepared by the optical frequency comb.

Laser parameters
The size of the probe, dressing, and coupling lasers were set to 750 \mu m, 800 \mu m, and 820 \mu m, respectively. The power of the probe, dressing, and coupling lasers were fixed to 1.5 \mu W, 11 mW, and 1 W, respectively. All powers were measured before the cell. The corresponding Rabi rates for the probe, dressing, and coupling are then 2\pi \times 700 kHz, 2\pi \times 8 MHz, and 2\pi \times 2.6 MHz, respectively. The powers of the probe and dressing lasers were stabilized using acousto-optic modulators. The power output of the coupling laser was not directly stabilized, but the fiber amplifier for the OPO pump was stabilized internally. The polarization of each of the lasers was set to be linear and vertical (relative to the optical table). The coupling laser polarization was optimized in order to minimize the central peak that forms from transitions not accessible by the RF fields.

Comb parameters
To produce the mid-infrared optical frequency comb we first generated an near-infrared frequency comb, which utilized an external-cavity diode laser (ECDL) as its source. The ECDL output was injected into a dual-drive Mach-Zehnder modulator (MZM). An 18 GHz signal generated by a RF source was split and each side was amplified to near 0.5 W before being sent to each side of the MZM. One side of the MZM had a 3 dB RF attenuator placed on it to achieve a flatter comb 43. The output of the MZM was an optical frequency comb with seven strong teeth which were spaced by 18 GHz. This comb was then amplified to 10 W by a fiber amplifier before being injected into a commercial, singly resonant, continuous-wave optical parametric oscillator (OPO). The OPO efficiently and coherently transfers the optical frequency comb to 2235 nm with an output power of more than 2 W 33,34.

Radio frequency parameters
To supply RF radiation to the atoms, we utilized three different horn antennas. An ETS 3115 antenna was used to cover 1 GHz to 18 GHz, we used a Narda 638 standard gain horn to cover 18 GHz to 26.5 GHz, and a Narda 637 standard gain horn to cover 26.5 GHz to 40 GHz (Certain equipment, instruments, software, or materials are identified in this paper in order to specify the experimental procedure adequately. Such identification is not intended to imply recommendation or endorsement of any product or service by NIST, nor is it intended to imply that the materials or equipment identified are necessarily the best available for the purpose). For the frequency scans, the power of the RF source for the 1 GHz to 18 GHz was fixed to 5 dBm, and the powers of the sources from 18 GHz to 40 GHz were fixed to 10 dBm. The difference was to optimize the visibility of the response between the two ranges. Each of the microwave horns were placed so that their polarization was linear and vertical (relative to the optical table).

Data acquisition
We scanned the coupling laser over 4 GHz at a scan rate of 30 Hz. We acquired 5 samples as the RF frequency or power was changed. The oscilloscope sampling rate was 2.5 GSa/s, making the frequency separation between points in the spectra 60 Hz in laser frequency. This is substantially below the linewidth and avoids electronic artifacts that can broaden the spectrum. In post-processing, we overlapped the data by using the 75P_{1/2} state since we did not scan over any resonant frequencies for that state.

## Paper

## Abstract

While Rydberg atoms have shown tremendous potential to serve as accurate and sensitive detectors of microwaves and millimeter waves, their response is generally limited to a single, narrow frequency band around a chosen transition. As a result, their potential to serve as agile and wideband electromagnetic receivers has not been fully realized. Here we demonstrate the use of a mid-infrared, frequency agile optical frequency comb as the coupling laser for three-photon Rydberg atom electrometry. This approach allows for rapid switching between as many as seven individual Rydberg states, allowing for multichannel detection across a frequency range from 1 GHz to 40 GHz. The generality and flexibility of this method for wideband multiplexing is anticipated to have transformative effects in the field of Rydberg electrometry, paving the way for advanced information coding, arbitrary signal detection, and the simultaneous detection of ultra-broadband radio frequency radiation.

---

## Introduction

Rydberg atoms have become ubiquitous in quantum-based technologies, including entangled ions and atoms for quantum computing, efficient microwave-to-optical conversion, and electric field sensing. Rydberg atoms offer large tuning bandwidths that range from DC to terahertz 1–5 and are highly sensitive to electric field variation and detection 6–15 as well as allowing for direct conversion 16–18 and phase sensing 7,8,19,20. However, unlike classical receivers that continuously monitor the entire spectrum of operation, the instantaneous bandwidth of Rydberg atom sensors is generally limited to tens of MHz around a selected carrier tone 8,17,21–24.

Typical sensitive field measurements utilize the resonant Autler–Townes (AT) effect to observe the response of the selected Rydberg state to external fields 4,25. The AT effect occurs when a field resonant with two states of the atoms perturbs and splits each of these energy levels, causing an observable change in the absorption signal of a probe laser. The probe laser is combined with a coupling laser and possible dressing lasers chosen to excite the atoms and readout the selected Rydberg state. The splitting frequency of this state is directly proportional to the magnitude of the radio frequency (RF) electric field given the dipole moment of the resonant RF transition. In this case, slow, coarse laser tuning by several nanometers is required to cover the full RF reception range 26. Complicated Rydberg engineering techniques can be employed to increase the RF bandwidth, but still does not bridge the gap for continuous measurements or multichannel detection of several incoming RF signals 27,28.

An alternative to the AT effect, the off-resonant Stark shift offers a near continuous tuning capability throughout the RF spectrum 5,29,30, however, with dramatically reduced sensitivity. Under the Stark shift condition, the RF field is far detuned (>100 MHz) from the resonance frequency between the two Rydberg states. Rather than inducing a splitting, this off-resonant field shifts the selected Rydberg state, and the frequency of this shift is proportional to the magnitude of the RF electric field squared times the polarizability of the state. A notable concern with this configuration is that information from multiple RF fields can be transferred onto a single probe laser, thus, generally leading to inseparable signals and limiting the total bandwidth of the system. For example, digital television antennas receive RF waves ranging from 50 MHz to 700 MHz and carry information with 6 MHz of modulation bandwidth. By demodulating the carrier after reception, several signals can be received and readout at the same time. However, with the off-resonant Stark shifting approach, these signals would be inseparable.

A major claim of Rydberg atom sensors has been their capacity for broadband sensing from DC to frequencies in the THz. However, current Rydberg sensors are only capable of achieving this through slow laser tuning and subsequent laser relocking. There is no published method to overcome the limited tuning capabilities of Rydberg atom sensors. Here, we have developed a method to remove this limitation that allows for the rapid preparation of up to seven different Rydberg states, with the potential for simultaneous operation in the future. These new capabilities pave the way towards advanced, broadband communication protocols, a long standing promise of Rydberg sensors that can be enabled by optical frequency combs.

Optical frequency combs have been transformative in wide-ranging fields such as time transfer, astronomy, and remote sensing 31,32. These advancements have largely leveraged the exquisite frequency accuracy that combs can provide as well as their wide spectral bandwidths. However, their low power per comb tooth (generally microwatts or even nanowatts) has proven limiting in some applications 33. Recently, we have demonstrated a new approach for spectral translation of electro-optic frequency combs using an optical parametric oscillator (OPO) 33,34. Critically, this method allows for highly coherent spectral translation from the near-infrared to the important mid-infrared spectral region with exceptionally high powers per comb tooth. Further, the resulting frequency combs are frequency-agile in that their comb spacing can be rapidly changed by adjusting the applied RF.

Here we utilize this frequency-agile optical frequency comb as the coupling laser in a three-photon Rydberg electrometry instrument, allowing for the rapid preparation of as many as seven Rydberg states. Further, we demonstrate that these seven individual states can provide orthogonal (i.e., independent) RF channels, which can allow for rapid and sensitive detection of a multitude of RF tones across a range from 1 GHz to 40 GHz, a range which was limited only by our available RF sources and antennas.

## Results

The multi-state Rydberg receiver described here relies upon three-photon excitation to generate and probe Rydberg states in cesium (Cs) atoms 35,36 as shown in Fig. 1. This three-photon configuration leads to reduced Doppler broadening due to the wavelengths of the three optical fields and theoretically a higher maximum sensitivity 35. Importantly, we note that the methods described here are equally applicable to more traditional two-photon approaches 37–40.

The coherent multi-photon process known as electromagnetically-induced absorption (EIA) allows for probing highly excited Rydberg states with higher precision than other methods such as ionization 26,41,42, electron beam ionization 42, and direct absorption 18. In the present three-photon process a 895 nm probe laser, a 636 nm dressing laser, and a 2235 nm coupling optical frequency comb are used in a successive excitation up to the Rydberg state(s) of interest, thus generating a coherent ensemble of atoms. The EIA is a result of this coherence, and the readout of the probe laser is a measure of the coherence between the ground state and the first excited state. The dressing and coupling laser modify this coherence through their interactions with the 9S intermediate state and the Rydberg state. This projection allows for measurements of Rydberg state(s) of interest by measuring the probe laser transmission. Similarly, modification of the Rydberg state by an RF field also affects the probe laser transmission.

We utilized an OPO to produce the frequency-agile, mid-infrared optical frequency comb 33,34 which served as the coupling laser (see Fig. 2). To generate this optical frequency comb, the 1068 nm OPO seed laser was first passed through a dual-drive Mach-Zehnder modulator 43. An optical frequency comb is produced with a comb spacing of 18 GHz by driving both sides of the modulator with an 18 GHz RF tone. This comb spacing was selected to roughly match the separation of the selected Rydberg states shown in Fig. 1b. The comb tooth amplitudes were then flattened by adjusting the phase shift and RF power between the two arms of the Mach-Zehnder modulator. The comb was then optically amplified to 10 W before serving as the pump laser for a singly resonant, continuous-wave OPO.

Because only the signal beam is resonant within the OPO cavity, the optical frequency comb on the pump beam was efficiently and coherently transferred onto the mid-infrared idler beam 33,34. Critically, this approach allows for the generation of a high power, frequency-agile comb, where the comb spacing and span are entirely flexible and can be set to well match an arbitrary set of Rydberg levels. In addition, the output comb can be tuned over a spectral range between 2200 nm and 4000 nm. For the present measurements, it was tuned to 2235 nm, where the comb had a total power >2 W and seven strong comb teeth which had an average power per tooth near 300 mW. This power per comb tooth was more than sufficient to allow for multi-state Rydberg preparation.

The optical frequency comb coupling laser was then combined with the 895 nm probe laser and passed through a 133 Cs filled vapor cell. The 636 nm dressing laser was counter-propagated through the cell to reduce the Doppler effect. The transmitted probe beam was then spectrally filtered (to remove the coupling light) and measured on a balanced photodiode, allowing for near shot-noise-limited detection.

As an initial demonstration, we scanned the OPO pump laser (and thus the entire coupling optical frequency comb) over a range of 4 GHz to excite each Rydberg state individually, as shown in Fig. 3a. The detuning of each state corresponds to the energy difference between the nearest comb tooth and the state in question (as defined in Table 1). The peaks in the spectrum show the seven Rydberg states which can be prepared by the optical frequency comb coupling laser. We note that the reverse configuration can also be performed. By locking the coupling laser and tuning the comb spacing 44, we could achieve fast switching between the distinct Rydberg states and employ a variety of demodulation schemes to receive information from the various frequency channels. While the comb spacing could theoretically be switched at gigahertz rates, the atomic lifetime of the intermediate state limits such switching to tens of MHz.

Armed with this multi-state readout, we can utilize this approach to observe a wide range of effects on the multitude of Rydberg states (see Fig. 1c) being probed. For example, we demonstrated the independent response of selected states to applied RF fields, the splitting of the Rydberg state resonances for calibration purposes, and even a Stark shift when the applied field is strong enough. Figure 3b shows the Autler–Townes splitting as the RF field strength is increased. We determined the field strength by extracting the splitting using the AT effect 4,

E = 2\pi\hbar\Delta_{meas} / \wp_{i,j} (1)

where \hbar is the reduced Planck constant, E is the electric field, \Delta_{meas} is the measured Rydberg state splitting, and \wp_{i,j} is the transition dipole moment between the two Rydberg states. For example, at -5 dBm of applied RF, we observe a splitting of 30 MHz. The transition dipole moment for this transition is 2480 e a_0, where e is the electron charge and a_0 is the Bohr radius. For this case, the field measured by the atoms was 0.95 V/m.

Figure 3b shows that as the field strength is decreased, we see the AT splitting decrease until the two peaks combine. As the splitting decreases the broadening from inhomogeneous fields also decreases 15. We are able to reduce the field down to 69 mV/m and still observe splitting. As the field is increased to large values (approaching 1 V/m) we can see that the splitting becomes so large that the split peaks can become difficult to observe. This is generally not limiting in Rydberg sensors, as there are techniques to minimize the inhomogeneities that cause broadening at strong fields and weak field measurements are not limited by these effects.

We note that if a modulated signal is used alongside lock-in detection (in order to reduce low-frequency noise), we can expect over two orders of magnitude improvement in the minimum detectable field 45. This would lead to an estimated sensitivity near 700 \mu V m^{-1} Hz^{-1/2}. However, this is far from a fundamental limitation for this sensor, as increased optical power would lead to corresponding increases in sensitivity.

We can also observe avoided crossings as the frequency of the applied RF is scanned (see Fig. 3c). The expected AT behavior with RF detuning is observed, in that there are three main effects on the observed splitting of the electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) signal 46: (1) the two peaks of the EIT signal are asymmetric, (2) the separation between the two AT peaks increases with RF detuning, and (3) one peak is pulled to the zero detuning location of the coupling laser. In this case, the splitting is proportional to the generalized Rabi frequency,

\Delta_{meas} = \sqrt{\Omega_{RF}^2 + \Delta_{RF}^2} (2)

where \Omega_{RF} is proportional to the field strength, \Delta_{RF} is the detuning of the RF frequency from the atomic resonance, and \Delta_{meas} is the measured splitting. We can use these avoided crossings to identify the location of the different RF Rydberg transitions. A central peak can be observed in this figure and this peak is a result of the relative polarization of the RF and optical fields. The discrepancy between Fig. 3b, c is due to the fact that they were taken on separate days and the polarization of the coupling laser may have been different. In general, we align the optical fields such that the polarization is vertically aligned relative to the table. The RF are similarly vertically polarized as well. However, with variations in mounts and optics on the table, reflections of the RF radiation could provide horizontally aligned polarization components causing the central peak to appear.

The unique broadband nature of the present method becomes apparent when different RF fields are applied to the atoms. For these measurements, we used three horn antennas to apply RF fields ranging from 1 GHz to 40 GHz. The lower RF bound was set by the atomic transitions between states in this region of the Rydberg manifold while the upper bound was set by the available RF sources and antennas. We note that the use of higher frequency RF sources and antennas should allow for a significantly wider measurable RF range.

For these measurements, we applied RF frequencies over 40-MHz-wide ranges which were centered on Rydberg transitions between 1 GHz and 40 GHz (see Fig. 4). For example, the first column in Fig. 4 shows the response of the seven states to a field ranging from 1.440 GHz to 1.480 GHz. A complete table of each of the different transition frequencies we can access is given in the Supplementary Table S1. For each column in Fig. 4 we highlight the panel where we expect a response to the RF field. We observed avoided crossings caused by the mixing of the optically excited Rydberg states and the Rydberg state coupled by the RF field 47.

The fits shown in the highlighted panels map the response of the Rydberg state energies using the generalized Rabi in Eq. (2). The energy of each dressed state present in AT splitting is given by the sum and difference of the generalized Rabi frequency and the detuning of the RF frequency from the atomic resonance,

\Delta_{\pm} = \Delta_{RF} \pm \sqrt{\Omega_{RF}^2 + \Delta_{RF}^2} / 2 (3)

where \Delta_{\pm} is the shift for each dressed state in MHz. From each highlighted panel, we extract the transmission for each given RF frequency and fit the data to find the energy of the two dressed states. We fit the dressed state energy separation as a function of RF detuning to obtain the fits seen. These fits can also be used to determine the strength of the RF field present at the atoms.

Importantly, since each of the transition frequencies in this section of the Rydberg manifold are separated by over 50 MHz (i.e., significantly greater than the <10 MHz response bandwidth of a given Rydberg state), a single RF frequency is expected to only interact with a single Rydberg state, thus allowing for complete orthogonality. Experimentally, this is what we observe, where the measured response to the RF fields in a multitude of different frequency bands up to 40 GHz exhibits no observable crosstalk between Rydberg states. This orthogonality condition is critical for communication protocols such as frequency hopping shared spectrum (FHSS) and orthogonal frequency domain multiplexing (OFDM).

FHSS is a protocol that relies on frequency-agile sensors that can quickly switch between frequency bands to avoid jamming or perform signal interception. However, the bands are generally limited by the bandwidth of the antenna being utilized for reception to, at most, a few gigahertz. Critically, with the present frequency comb-based approach, it should be possible to switch between vastly different operational bands and therefore significantly improve the performance of this protocol for Rydberg sensing. FHSS does not require simultaneous measurements but instead relies on rapid switching between different bands that contain segments of the full spectrum of information. With fast tuning of the comb teeth and the orthogonality of the channels, we should be able to demonstrate this protocol with our current system. Furthermore, we could cover a range of frequencies that normally require at least 5 different antennas and sets of mixers to receive and analyze.

OFDM is another protocol that relies upon spreading information over several frequency bands simultaneously. In this way, information is simultaneously sent over multiple carriers, and each carrier must be separately demodulated. While the FHSS protocol can be achieved by utilizing Stark shifting measurements, OFDM requires that all carriers be received simultaneously and typically have the same base-band modulation (i.e., the carriers must be separable). In the case that a single probe readout were used in conjunction with Stark shifting measurements, all of the base bands would interfere. This is where the present frequency comb method would separate the RF carriers for simultaneous broadband detection. While the system demonstrated here cannot presently perform this protocol, it paves the way for this enhanced capability.

We note that a major advantage of the present approach over traditional, classical implementations of OFDM and FHSS is the capability of sensing over multiple bands. For a classical antenna, the measurement band is limited, and the antenna is typically engineered to accept specific frequencies with matching circuits in order to optimize performance at a particular frequency. This leads to measurement bands which are normally limited to within 1 GHz of the center. Rydberg atoms allow for measurements over vastly different bands separated by nearly 40 GHz in the present demonstration, and nearly 1 THz in the future. This represents a paradigm shift from classical receivers and opens the door for new methods of secure communication.

While the RF channels are connected to separate Rydberg states and therefore, to avoid cross-talk, this information is projected onto a single probe laser. This will result in a mixing of the different RF channels. To avoid this, we must incorporate a comb onto the probe and dressing lasers to match the energy difference of the comb teeth of the coupling laser and the Rydberg states of interest. However, we are concerned with the information being mixed through the narrow-band 9S intermediate state.

In future work, we will place a comb on the coupling laser in a more traditional two-photon system. In addition, we can place a comb on the probe laser 48 to compensate the energy, giving us access to the full Doppler width. The probe would have a comb that matches the detunings present on the scan of the coupling laser. This approach would allow for simultaneous state preparation and the protocols such as OFDM.

Further, the present approach provides a pathway toward a dramatic increase in the response bandwidth of Rydberg atoms sensors. By using simultaneous state readout (such as OFDM) in concert with our optical frequency comb-based approach, we should be able to demonstrate a bandwidth that scales with the number of comb teeth 49. With our current demonstration, it should be possible to demonstrate 100 MHz of bandwidth if we incorporate the nP_{1/2} states.

The use of an optical frequency comb as the coupling laser for Rydberg electrometry enables rapid and orthogonal measurements over a range of states and therefore radio frequencies. The increased capabilities made possible by this approach are expected to have an extensive impact on communications and sensing. We note that a classical receiver would require numerous different antennas and substantial down-conversion hardware to receive the same signals that this comb-enabled Rydberg receiver can readily record. Further, for the present demonstration, we recorded radio frequencies from 1 GHz to 40 GHz; however, extending this range to 100 GHz is readily possible, whereby the direct conversion nature of Rydberg atoms is anticipated to be truly enabling as telecommunications continue to push the limits of existing electronic hardware.

## Methods

Laser stabilization
The 895 nm probe laser frequency was stabilized using saturated absorption spectroscopy to the 6S_{1/2}, F=4 \rightarrow 6P_{1/2}, F=3 transition. A portion of the 895 nm probe and the 636 nm dressing lasers were utilized to generate a two-photon EIT. The 636 nm dressing laser was tuned and locked to the 6P_{1/2}, F=3 \rightarrow 9S_{1/2}, F=4 transition using the two-photon EIT. The 2235 nm coupling laser was free running and scanned over 4 GHz to access the various Rydberg states prepared by the optical frequency comb.

Laser parameters
The size of the probe, dressing, and coupling lasers were set to 750 \mu m, 800 \mu m, and 820 \mu m, respectively. The power of the probe, dressing, and coupling lasers were fixed to 1.5 \mu W, 11 mW, and 1 W, respectively. All powers were measured before the cell. The corresponding Rabi rates for the probe, dressing, and coupling are then 2\pi \times 700 kHz, 2\pi \times 8 MHz, and 2\pi \times 2.6 MHz, respectively. The powers of the probe and dressing lasers were stabilized using acousto-optic modulators. The power output of the coupling laser was not directly stabilized, but the fiber amplifier for the OPO pump was stabilized internally. The polarization of each of the lasers was set to be linear and vertical (relative to the optical table). The coupling laser polarization was optimized in order to minimize the central peak that forms from transitions not accessible by the RF fields.

Comb parameters
To produce the mid-infrared optical frequency comb we first generated an near-infrared frequency comb, which utilized an external-cavity diode laser (ECDL) as its source. The ECDL output was injected into a dual-drive Mach-Zehnder modulator (MZM). An 18 GHz signal generated by a RF source was split and each side was amplified to near 0.5 W before being sent to each side of the MZM. One side of the MZM had a 3 dB RF attenuator placed on it to achieve a flatter comb 43. The output of the MZM was an optical frequency comb with seven strong teeth which were spaced by 18 GHz. This comb was then amplified to 10 W by a fiber amplifier before being injected into a commercial, singly resonant, continuous-wave optical parametric oscillator (OPO). The OPO efficiently and coherently transfers the optical frequency comb to 2235 nm with an output power of more than 2 W 33,34.

Radio frequency parameters
To supply RF radiation to the atoms, we utilized three different horn antennas. An ETS 3115 antenna was used to cover 1 GHz to 18 GHz, we used a Narda 638 standard gain horn to cover 18 GHz to 26.5 GHz, and a Narda 637 standard gain horn to cover 26.5 GHz to 40 GHz (Certain equipment, instruments, software, or materials are identified in this paper in order to specify the experimental procedure adequately. Such identification is not intended to imply recommendation or endorsement of any product or service by NIST, nor is it intended to imply that the materials or equipment identified are necessarily the best available for the purpose). For the frequency scans, the power of the RF source for the 1 GHz to 18 GHz was fixed to 5 dBm, and the powers of the sources from 18 GHz to 40 GHz were fixed to 10 dBm. The difference was to optimize the visibility of the response between the two ranges. Each of the microwave horns were placed so that their polarization was linear and vertical (relative to the optical table).

Data acquisition
We scanned the coupling laser over 4 GHz at a scan rate of 30 Hz. We acquired 5 samples as the RF frequency or power was changed. The oscilloscope sampling rate was 2.5 GSa/s, making the frequency separation between points in the spectra 60 Hz in laser frequency. This is substantially below the linewidth and avoids electronic artifacts that can broaden the spectrum. In post-processing, we overlapped the data by using the 75P_{1/2} state since we did not scan over any resonant frequencies for that state.

In Fig. 4, panel 73 P3/2 @ 30 GHz, what is the reason for the central resonance (the horizontal yellow

This line is due to the polarization of the RF relative to the lasers. If the polarization is mismatched,
there will be magnetic sublevels that do not shift in response to the RF. However, this will only be seen
for P→S transitions and not P→D transitions of the RF field (as shown in
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.17997, shown below). We utilized several horns with slight variations in
angles relative to the atoms. This likely caused variations in the polarization that are most obvious in
the high frequency horn. For example, the 30 GHz transition for 73P is to an S state, while the 35
GHz transition for the panel for 75P is a transition to a D state, and we do not see the central peak.
While we set the polarizations of the horns and lasers to minimize this peak, reflections and scattering
of the RF can cause the peak to appear and be strong.

Long and co-workers use a remarkable frequency comb (300 mW per tooth at 2.2 microns!) to demonstrate
a Rydberg microwave receiver that can be quickly tuned to any number of Autler-Townes resonances. The
experimental results confirm the basic ideas and the discussion and analysis make a strong case that the
method will be efficacious for various communication modes.
What is curious to me are the extremely large RF levels that are detected in the experiment. They state,
"Further, we demonstrate that the seven individual states can provide orthogonal RF channels, allowing
for simultaneous and highly sensitive detection of a multitude of RF tones". Perhaps the wording is carefully
saying that the only thing they have actually done is show the orthogonality, and that with future work it
could become highly sensitive.

many orders of magnitude higher than typical Rydberg sensor sensitivities. I understand that the real
argument for this method is that a comparable classical technology would require an array of antennas, so
perhaps it is not the sensitivity that is the issue. Nevertheless, the fields they used are very large. Also

have the impact suggested by the authors. Furthermore, I doubt that the complexity of a (very cool) state of
the art OPO frequency comb system is less than a classical antenna array.

system has a Doppler canceling that the two-photon systems do not and can achieve very narrow
lines. So, in the sentence where we state “highly sensitive detection”, we have added “theoretically”
to avoid ambiguity of the measurement. The standard two-photon system can achieve 5
𝛍𝐕𝐦−𝟏𝐇𝐳−𝟏/𝟐 sensitivity. This is achieved by using a mixer approach with the atoms and looking at

of-fluorescence-versus-transmission”
